title: Open the Lock
description: Brute force to optimized: a list-based level-by-level BFS versus the standard true-queue BFS pattern, checking the target immediately upon discovery.

blocks.text: A lock has 4 circular wheels, each with digits 0-9 (wrapping: 9 turns to 0, 0 turns to 9). Each move turns ONE wheel by ONE slot. The lock starts at "0000". Given a list of deadends (if the lock ever displays one of these, it becomes permanently stuck), return the MINIMUM number of moves to reach target, or -1 if impossible.

blocks.caption: Each 4-digit state is a node in an implicit graph; a BFS explores states level by level, guaranteeing the first time target is reached uses the minimum number of moves

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of deadend states, and a target state"],["Output","The minimum number of moves to reach target from \"0000\", avoiding deadends, or -1 if impossible"],["Goal","Find the shortest path in an implicit graph where each 4-digit combination is a node"],["Constraints","1 <= deadends.length <= 500; deadends[i].length == 4; target.length == 4; target is not in deadends; target != \"0000\""]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"MINIMUM number of moves/turns\" to reach a target state","Breadth-first search (BFS), which explores states in order of increasing distance, guaranteeing the FIRST time a target is reached uses the fewest moves"],["Each state has a FIXED, small set of possible next states (8 neighbors per state)","The graph is entirely IMPLICIT: states and edges (neighbors) are generated on the fly, rather than being given explicitly"]]}

blocks.text: Every possible 4-digit combination ("0000" through "9999") can be thought of as a NODE in a graph, with an EDGE between two states if they differ by exactly one wheel turned one position (accounting for wrap-around); finding the minimum number of moves is exactly finding the SHORTEST PATH from "0000" to target in this implicit graph, avoiding deadend nodes entirely.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Shortest Sequence of Single Dial-Turns on a Combination Lock
blocks.text: Imagine a physical combination lock with 4 dials, and wanting the fewest possible single-dial-turns to go from the starting combination to a target combination, while never landing on any of several "trap" combinations along the way (which would jam the lock). Since every single turn is an equally-weighted, equally-costed step, exploring outward from the start ONE TURN AT A TIME, level by level, guarantees the target (once first reached) was reached using the fewest possible turns.

blocks.caption: Each state has exactly 8 neighbors (each of 4 wheels turned +1 or -1); BFS explores these level by level, so the level at which target is found is the minimum number of turns

blocks.text: Example: deadends = many combinations surrounding "8888", target = "8888"

blocks.text: Before exploring randomly or using depth-first search (which does not guarantee finding the SHORTEST path first), notice that breadth-first search, exploring states in order of increasing distance from the start, guarantees the first time the target is reached, it is via the minimum number of moves.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since every single move costs EXACTLY one turn (no move is "cheaper" than another), the problem is precisely an UNWEIGHTED shortest-path problem, for which BFS is the standard, provably-correct technique.

Observation 2: Each state (a 4-digit string) has EXACTLY 8 possible next states: each of the 4 wheels, turned either +1 or -1 (with wrap-around at 9/0).

Observation 3: BFS explores states in "waves" (levels): all states reachable in 1 move, then all states reachable in 2 moves, and so on; the FIRST wave in which the target appears directly gives the minimum number of moves.

Observation 4: A visited set prevents revisiting the SAME state multiple times (which would be wasteful and could even cause infinite loops), and deadend states are simply treated as ALREADY visited from the very start (never explored at all).

Observation 5: The graph itself is never explicitly built; each state's neighbors are generated ON THE FLY as needed, which is both simpler and more memory-efficient than precomputing the entire graph.
This is a standard BFS on an implicit graph, where each 4-digit combination is a node, and single-wheel-turns are the edges; BFS guarantees the shortest path (minimum number of moves) is found.

Perform BFS level by level, but using a plain LIST as the frontier (rebuilt fresh each level) rather than a true queue; still correct, but less idiomatic and slightly less efficient than a proper queue-based implementation.

items: Maintain a "frontier" list of states reachable in the current number of moves, starting with just "0000".

At each level, check if target is in the current frontier (return the current step count if so); otherwise, build the NEXT frontier from all unvisited, non-deadend neighbors of the current frontier's states.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Processing states level by level (rebuilding a fresh "next frontier" list) directly implements the core BFS idea of exploring by increasing distance.
Checking "is target in the current frontier" (an O(n) list scan) works, but is less efficient than the standard queue-based BFS pattern, which checks each state as it is dequeued.

blocks.text: Correctly finds the minimum number of moves, since it explores states in the correct level-by-level order.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(10^4) states, each with 8 neighbors, so O(10^4 * 8) overall; the "is target in frontier" list scan adds some inefficiency but does not change the overall complexity class.
Space: O(10^4), for the visited set and frontier lists.

Limitation: using a plain list as the frontier (with an O(n) "contains" check) is less idiomatic and slightly less efficient than a true queue-based BFS, which checks the target condition as each state is individually dequeued.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force uses a plain list for the frontier. Instead, use a TRUE queue (with O(1) enqueue/dequeue), processing one full BFS level at a time (tracked by the queue's size at the start of each level). Check whether a newly-discovered neighbor IS the target immediately upon generating it, returning the current step count right away, rather than scanning the whole frontier afterward.

Handle the "0000" is a deadend" and "target is 0000" edge cases directly. Otherwise, initialize a queue with "0000" and a visited set. While the queue is non-empty: record the current queue size (this level's node count), increment steps, then process exactly that many nodes: for each, generate its 8 neighbors, skipping deadends and already-visited states; if a neighbor equals target, return steps immediately; otherwise, mark it visited and enqueue it.
Use a true queue-based BFS, processing one level at a time, checking for the target as each neighbor is generated.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: 1, matching the expected result: the target is found on the very first level explored.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(10^4 * 8) = O(1) (bounded by a small constant, since there are only 10^4 possible 4-digit states total).
Space: O(10^4), for the visited set and queue.

BFS explores states in STRICTLY increasing order of distance from the start: every state at "distance k" (reachable in exactly k moves) is fully processed before any state at "distance k+1" is even considered. This guarantees that the FIRST time target is encountered (as a neighbor being generated), it is via the SHORTEST possible path, since a shorter path would have already caused it to be discovered at an earlier level.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["\"0000\" itself is a deadend","Immediately impossible: return -1 without any search"],["target equals \"0000\"","Trivially reachable in 0 moves: return 0 immediately"],["A generated neighbor equals target","Return the CURRENT level's step count immediately, which is guaranteed to be the minimum"]]}

items: Processing "one full level at a time" (using the queue's SIZE at the start of each level as a loop bound) is the key mechanism that correctly tracks HOW MANY moves have been made so far.
Checking "is this newly generated neighbor the target" immediately (before even enqueueing it) allows returning as soon as possible, without needing a separate final scan.
The visited set (seeded with "0000" from the start) prevents ever revisiting the same state, which would otherwise cause redundant work or even infinite loops.

blocks.text: "Minimum number of moves/steps" to reach a target state, where each move has EQUAL cost, is the defining signal for BFS on an implicit graph, where states are nodes generated on the fly and BFS's level-by-level exploration guarantees the shortest path is found first.

items: Forgetting the wrap-around rule (9 turns to 0, 0 turns to 9) when generating neighbors.
Not checking whether the STARTING state ("0000") is itself a deadend, which should immediately make the problem unsolvable.
Using DFS instead of BFS, which does not guarantee finding the shortest path first (it might find a much longer path to the target before a shorter one).

items: Explicitly stating "this is BFS on an IMPLICIT graph, since states and edges are generated on the fly rather than given explicitly" demonstrates recognizing the underlying graph structure clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Minimum number of moves/turns/steps to reach a target state" (with equal-cost moves) points directly to BFS, typically on an implicit graph of states.

items: How would you optimize this further using BIDIRECTIONAL BFS (searching from both "0000" and target simultaneously)? Meeting in the middle can significantly reduce the number of states explored, especially when the search space is large, though it adds implementation complexity.
How would this change if some wheel turns had different COSTS (not all equal to 1)? BFS would no longer directly apply; a weighted shortest-path algorithm like Dijkstra's would be needed instead.

What is the theoretical maximum number of states that could ever be explored? Exactly 10^4 (all four-digit combinations from "0000" to "9999"), bounding the entire search regardless of the specific deadends or target.

A classic "BFS on an implicit state graph" problem, structurally similar to Shortest Path in Binary Matrix elsewhere in this category, both using BFS to find a shortest path where states/positions and their neighbors are generated on the fly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(10^4 * 8) time, O(10^4) space.
Optimized (true queue, level-by-level BFS): O(10^4 * 8) time, O(10^4) space (same complexity class, cleaner implementation).

items: Pattern: Breadth-first search (BFS) on an implicit state graph

Core Idea: Each 4-digit combination is a node; BFS explores states level by level (one queue-size's worth of nodes per level), guaranteeing the first time target is found, it is via the minimum number of moves
Time: O(10^4 * 8), bounded by the total number of possible states
Space: O(10^4)
Most Important Observation: Every move has EQUAL cost, making this an unweighted shortest-path problem, for which BFS is the standard, provably-correct technique
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: BFS from "0000"; each state has 8 neighbors (each wheel +1/-1, wrapping); return the level where target is first found
